competencies.title: Can mix new colours from primary colours
Can keep a steady beat and copy a rhythm
Can tell a story with a beginning, middle and end
Can make 5 crafts from recycled materials
Can draw an object from observation
Can design and prototype a solution to a brief
Can compose a short piece of music
Can build and present a creative portfolio

items.subject: painting
items.title: Magic colour mixing
items.summary: Mix two colours. A new colour appears!
steps: 👕 Put on an old shirt.
🟡🔵 Put a blob of yellow and a blob of blue on a plate.
👆 Mix them with your finger or a brush. What colour now? 🟢 Green!
🔴🟡 Try red and yellow. 🟠 Orange!
🔴🔵 Try red and blue. 🟣 Purple!
🎨 Paint a picture with your new colours.

safety.notes: Use child-safe, washable paint. An adult stays nearby. Wash hands after. Keep paint away from mouth and eyes.

materials: Food colouring or fruit juice in water
basic.description: Mix coloured water from beetroot, turmeric or berry juice on paper.

materials: Red, yellow and blue washable paint
better.description: Mix the three primary colours to make orange, green and purple.

materials: Paint set with white and black
advanced.description: Add white to make light colours and a tiny bit of black to make dark ones.

substitutions.use: Water with food colouring, turmeric (yellow), beetroot juice (pink) or cold tea (brown)
Fingers, a cotton bud or a twig

check.question: Yellow and blue make...
check.explain: Yes! Yellow and blue make green, like leaves.

check.question: Red and yellow make...
check.explain: Orange, like an orange!

items.subject: music
items.title: Clap the beat
items.summary: Clap, tap and stomp to a song.
steps: Sing a song you know together.
Clap along with every beat.
Now tap your knees instead.
Now stomp your feet!
Grown-up claps a little pattern. Can you copy it?

check.question: What can you clap with?
check.explain: Clap, clap! Hands make a great drum.

check.question: Can feet make music too?
check.explain: Stomping is a big, loud beat!

items.adultNote: Start slowly. Short patterns (clap-clap-pause) are best at this age. Clear some floor space for stomping.

items.subject: storytelling
items.title: Tell a picture story
items.summary: Pick a toy. Tell a story about it. What happens next?
steps: Choose a toy. That is your hero!
Where does it live?
Something happens! Maybe it gets lost.
How does it feel? Happy, sad, scared?
How does the story end?
Draw your story if you like.

check.question: A story has a start, a middle and...
check.explain: Every story has an end. What was yours?

check.question: Can a hero feel scared?
check.explain: Yes. Heroes have feelings too, and that makes stories exciting.

items.adultNote: Ask "and then what happened?" to keep the story going. Write down the child's words to read back later.

items.subject: crafts
items.title: Paper plate animal mask
items.summary: Cut, stick and paint an animal mask, then act like your animal.
steps: Choose an animal.
An adult marks eye holes on a paper plate. Cut them out with round-tip scissors (an adult starts the hole).
Cut ears and a nose from scrap card and glue them on.
Colour or paint your mask.
Tie string or tape a stick to the side to hold it.
Act out how your animal moves and sounds.

hazards: Glue on skin or in eyes
safety.notes: Use round-tip child scissors and cut away from your body. An adult starts the eye holes. Use non-toxic glue. Do not tie string around the neck; hold the mask on a stick or tie behind the head loosely, and take it off before running.

materials: Paper plate or cereal box card
basic.description: Make the mask from a cereal box and colour it with pencil.

advanced.description: Add texture with wool or fabric and an elastic strap, then make masks for a short play.

substitutions.use: Flour and water paste (mix 1 spoon flour with a little water)
Card cut from a cereal box

check.question: When using scissors, cut...
check.explain: Cutting away keeps fingers safe.

check.question: What can you use if there is no glue?
check.explain: Flour paste sticks paper well and is cheap.

items.subject: music
items.title: Make a shaker
items.summary: Make a shaker from a bottle and dried rice, then play a rhythm.
steps: Wash and dry a small plastic bottle.
Pour in a few spoons of dried rice or beans.
Close the lid tightly. An adult tapes it shut.
Shake it! Try fast, slow, loud and quiet.
Fill another bottle with something else. Does it sound different?
Play along to a song: shake on every beat.

hazards: Dried beans or rice can choke small children
safety.notes: Tape the lid shut so it cannot open. Keep shakers and loose beans away from babies and toddlers. Sweep up spills.

materials: Dried rice, lentils or small stones
basic.description: One bottle shaker with tape on the lid.

better.description: Make two shakers with different sounds and decorate them.

advanced.description: Make a home band: shaker, box guitar with rubber bands and a pot drum.

substitutions.use: Two paper cups taped together, or a tin with a lid
Small pebbles, buttons or bottle caps

check.question: More rice in the bottle makes the sound...
check.explain: More grains hit the sides, making a fuller sound.

check.question: Why tape the lid?
options: So small pieces cannot spill out
check.explain: Loose beans can be a choking danger for little ones.

items.subject: drawing
items.title: Draw what you see
items.summary: Look closely at one fruit and draw exactly what you see, not what you think it looks like.
steps: Put one fruit on the table in front of you.
Look for one minute without drawing. What shapes do you see?
Draw the outline lightly.
Look again: where is it lighter? Where is it darker?
Add the stalk, spots and the shadow on the table.
Compare with the real fruit. What did you notice that you never saw before?

safety.notes: An adult sharpens pencils for younger children. Sit at a table with good light.

basic.description: One pencil drawing of one object.

better.description: Draw the same object three times from different sides.

advanced.description: Keep a weekly sketchbook of observational drawings.

substitutions.use: The back of used paper or cardboard
Draw lightly first, then go over good lines darker

check.question: Before drawing, it helps to...
check.explain: Artists spend more time looking than drawing.

check.question: The side away from the light looks...
check.explain: Shadow shows the shape is round.

items.subject: storytelling
items.title: Make a comic strip
items.summary: Tell a short story in six panels with pictures and speech bubbles.
steps: Fold a sheet of paper into six boxes.
Plan: a character, a problem and how it is solved.
Panel 1 shows the character. Panels 2 to 5 show the problem growing. Panel 6 solves it.
Draw simple figures. Stick people are fine!
Add speech bubbles and sound words like CRASH!
Share it and ask what the reader thought would happen next.

check.question: A speech bubble shows...
check.explain: The tail points to whoever is speaking.

check.question: A thought bubble usually looks like...
check.explain: Cloud bubbles show what a character thinks.

items.subject: drama
items.title: Freeze-frame drama
items.summary: Make a frozen picture with your body to show a moment from a story.
steps: Choose a scene from a story you know.
Decide who each person is.
Count 3, 2, 1, freeze! Hold a still pose that shows the moment.
Use your face to show feelings.
The audience guesses what is happening.
Unfreeze one character to say one line.

check.question: In a freeze-frame you...
check.explain: Still bodies and clear faces tell the story.

check.question: How can you show a character is worried?
check.explain: Hunched shoulders and a frown say a lot without words.

items.adultNote: Works with one child (the adult joins in) or a group. Clear a space free of sharp corners.

items.subject: music
items.title: Read and write rhythms
items.summary: Write rhythms with simple symbols and clap them back.
steps: Learn: a crotchet (quarter note) is one beat: say "ta". Two quavers (eighth notes) share one beat: say "ti-ti". A rest is one beat of silence.
Clap: ta ta ti-ti ta.
Write a 4-beat rhythm using ta, ti-ti and rest.
Swap rhythms with someone and clap theirs.
Put four rhythms together to make a 16-beat piece and play it on a shaker or pot.

check.question: How many beats do two quavers (ti-ti) take?
check.explain: Two quavers share one beat: half a beat each.

check.question: ta, ti-ti, rest, ta has how many beats?

items.subject: drawing
items.title: One-point perspective street
items.summary: Draw a street that seems to go into the distance, using a horizon line and a vanishing point.
steps: Draw a horizon line across the middle of the page.
Put one dot on it: the vanishing point.
Draw the road edges as two lines meeting at the dot.
Draw building fronts as rectangles, then join their corners to the dot.
Add windows and doors that get smaller as they get closer to the dot.
Look out of a window and find real vanishing lines.

check.question: In one-point perspective, lines going away from you meet at...
check.explain: All depth lines head to one point on the horizon.

check.question: Objects further away are drawn...
check.explain: Smaller size creates the illusion of distance.

items.subject: design
items.title: Design and build a desk organiser
items.summary: Use the design process to make a cardboard organiser for someone at home.
steps: Interview your user: what do they need to store and where?
Write a design brief: who, what, size limits, materials.
Sketch three different ideas and choose one with your user.
Make a paper model first to test the size.
Measure and mark the cardboard. Cut with an adult supervising the craft knife on a cutting board, or use strong scissors.
Assemble with glue or tape, test with the real items and improve one thing.

safety.notes: An adult supervises any craft knife use. Cut on a board, with the blade moving away from your body and fingers behind the blade, and retract or cap the blade every time you put it down. Scissors are the safer option. If using a hot glue gun, the adult sets it up and you do not touch the nozzle.

basic.description: Cut down boxes and tubes and stick them together.

materials: Safety ruler and craft knife (adult supervised)
better.description: Measured, straight-cut parts with slots or glued joints.

materials: Thick card or thin plywood offcuts
advanced.description: A finished, painted organiser with dividers sized from measurements of the real items.

substitutions.use: A thick old magazine or wooden board

sources.title: Home and leisure safety
sources.publisher: Royal Society for the Prevention of Accidents (RoSPA)

check.question: Why build a paper model first?
options: To test the idea cheaply before the real build
check.explain: Prototypes catch problems early.

check.question: When you put a craft knife down you should...
check.explain: A covered blade cannot cut anyone by accident.

check.question: A design brief describes...
options: who it is for and what it must do
check.explain: A brief keeps the design focused on the user.

items.adultNote: Supervise any blade or hot glue. Scissors are fine for the whole project if you prefer.

items.subject: music
items.title: Compose a short melody
items.summary: Write an 8-bar tune using five notes, then perform or record it.
steps: Use five notes: C D E G A (the pentatonic scale). Any instrument, glasses of water or a free app works. You can also sing them.
Make a 2-bar idea (a motif).
Repeat it, then change it a little.
Write a contrasting middle section and end back on C so it feels finished.
Write it down with letter names and rhythm symbols.
Perform or record it and ask a listener what mood it has.

check.question: A motif is...
options: a short musical idea that can repeat
check.explain: Composers build whole pieces from motifs.

check.question: Ending on the home note (C here) makes the tune feel...
check.explain: The home note gives a sense of arrival.

items.adultNote: No instrument? Glasses filled with different amounts of water make tuned notes, and voices are an instrument too.

items.subject: design
items.title: Design a clear poster
items.summary: Use contrast, alignment, repetition, hierarchy and space to make a poster people understand in three seconds.
steps: Pick a real message, e.g. a local event or a safety reminder.
Decide the one thing a viewer must notice first (hierarchy).
Sketch three layouts using a grid.
Apply contrast (big vs small, dark vs light), alignment and repetition.
Leave empty space so it can breathe.
Test: show it to someone for three seconds. What did they remember? Revise.

check.question: Hierarchy in design means...
options: making the most important thing stand out first
check.explain: Size, weight and position guide the eye in order.

check.question: Why leave empty space?
options: It helps the important parts stand out
check.explain: White space reduces clutter and improves clarity.

items.subject: drama
items.title: Write and stage a short scene
items.summary: Write a two-character scene with conflict and stage directions, then rehearse and perform it.
steps: Choose two characters who want different things.
Write a 2-page script: names, dialogue and short stage directions in brackets.
Read it aloud and cut any line that does not move the scene forward.
Block it: decide where each actor stands and moves.
Rehearse three times, then perform or film it.
Reflect: what would you change for a second version?

check.question: Stage directions tell actors...
options: what to do and how to move
check.explain: They usually appear in brackets or italics.

check.question: Drama usually needs...
check.explain: Conflict creates tension and interest.

items.adultNote: If filming, only share with the performers' permission and never post publicly without parental consent.

items.subject: portfolio
items.title: Build a creative portfolio
items.summary: Select, improve and present 8 to 12 pieces that show your range, process and growth.
steps: Gather everything you have made: drawings, designs, music, scripts, crafts.
Choose 8 to 12 pieces that show range and your best work.
Include process: one page of sketches or drafts for at least two pieces.
Write a short caption for each: title, materials, date, what you were trying to do.
Arrange them in an order that tells a story about you.
Present it to someone and ask for feedback. Photograph or scan the final set if you can.

hazards: Craft tools used while repairing or mounting work
safety.notes: Use the same tool safety as each original piece. Only share your portfolio online with a trusted adult's agreement, and leave out personal details such as your address or school.

materials: A folder made from folded card
basic.description: A hand-made folder of work with written captions.

better.description: A neat binder with sections, captions and process pages.

advanced.description: A digital portfolio with photographs of each piece and a short artist statement.

substitutions.use: Two pieces of cardboard taped along one edge
Photographs taken in daylight near a window

check.question: Why include process work (sketches, drafts)?
options: It shows how you think and improve
check.explain: Viewers value seeing how ideas develop.

check.question: A good portfolio has...
check.explain: Selecting shows judgement.

items.subject: puppets
items.title: Sock puppet friend
items.summary: Turn an old sock into a puppet friend. Make it talk and sing!
steps: 🧦 Find an old, clean sock.
✋ Put your hand inside.
👀 Draw or stick on eyes and a mouth.
🗣️ Give your puppet a name.
🎭 Make your puppet say hello!

hazards: buttons and googly eyes are a choking risk
safety.notes: Use paper eyes or drawn eyes, not buttons, for under-fives. Use child-safe glue and wash hands afterwards.

basic.description: Draw a face on a sock.

better.description: Add paper ears and wool hair.

advanced.description: Make a puppet family and a box theatre for a show.

substitutions.use: a paper bag or a glove
a little flour-and-water paste or tape

check.question: Your puppet needs eyes. Use...
check.explain: Yes! Paper eyes are safe and fun.

check.question: How is your puppet feeling?
check.explain: Any answer is right! Puppets can have every feeling.

items.adultNote: Talk to the puppet, not the child: shy children often answer through a puppet. Use puppets later to talk about feelings or new situations.

items.subject: drawing
items.title: Leaf rubbing magic
items.summary: Put a leaf under paper. Rub with a crayon. Watch the leaf appear!
steps: 🍂 Pick up a fallen leaf with a grown-up.
📄 Put the leaf under a sheet of paper.
🖍️ Rub the side of a crayon over it.
✨ Look! The lines of the leaf appear.
🌈 Try another leaf and another colour.

hazards: unknown plants can sting or irritate skin
safety.notes: Collect only fallen leaves an adult says are safe. Do not pick living plants or put leaves in mouths. Wash hands afterwards.

materials: crayons with the paper peeled off
better.description: Many leaves and colours on one page.

advanced.description: Rub other bumpy things too and guess what made each pattern.

substitutions.use: a coin, a comb, a bumpy mat or a flat key
a soft pencil on its side or charcoal

check.question: Which leaves can we use?
check.explain: Yes! Fallen leaves are free, and the tree keeps growing.

check.question: Rub with the...
check.explain: Yes! The side of the crayon shows the lines best.

items.adultNote: Peel the paper off old crayons and use them on their side. Hold the paper still for small hands. Name the shapes and lines you see together.

items.subject: design
items.title: Floor pattern art
items.summary: People in many places make patterns on floors and doorsteps. Design your own pattern with dots, lines and colour.
steps: Look at patterns around you: tiles, cloth, flowers.
Make a grid of dots on paper or the ground: 5 rows of 5.
Join the dots with lines and curves to make a shape.
Repeat the shape so the pattern is the same on both sides.
Add colour with chalk, petals, leaves or coloured powder.
Take a photo or draw it, because floor art does not last!

safety.notes: Work in a spot where people do not walk. Sweep up when finished. Do not blow powder near faces.

materials: Paper and pencil, or a stick and a patch of earth
basic.description: Draw a dot-grid pattern on paper or in soil.

better.description: Make a small pattern on a step or path with chalk lines and natural colour.

advanced.description: Design a large pattern with a family member, plan it on paper first, then make it together.

substitutions.use: Flour or rice flour sprinkled from a paper cone
Fallen petals, leaves, sand, seeds or small stones

items.adultNote: Floor and doorstep patterns are made in many cultures, for example rangoli and kolam in India and sand or tile patterns elsewhere. Use only fallen petals, and choose a spot that can be swept.

items.subject: storytelling
items.title: Sound effects story
items.summary: Tell a story and add the sounds with your voice, hands and feet. Rain, footsteps, a door creak!
steps: Pick a short story, or make one up about a walk in the rain.
List the sounds in it: wind, rain, footsteps, a dog barking.
Find a way to make each sound: rub hands, tap fingers, stamp feet.
Practise each sound loud and soft.
Tell the story while a helper makes the sounds, then swap.
Perform it for your family.

check.question: How could you make the sound of light rain?
options: Tap your fingertips softly on a table
Shout as loud as you can
check.explain: Soft, fast taps sound like raindrops. Louder taps sound like heavy rain.

items.adultNote: No equipment is needed. This builds listening, timing and confidence speaking in front of others.
